title: Helping a colleague
hookLine: the Buddha washes a sick monk the others left alone: service at your desk
tomorrow: even God stopped working. how did he know it was done?

lines: SICK, ALONE, NO USE TO THE OTHERS.
cards: At work there's often someone who isn't quite anyone's job: the new hire, the temp, the one from another team. The Vinaya, the Buddhist rules for monks, tells of a monk like that.

He's sick with dysentery, lying in his own filth, alone. The Buddha comes by with his attendant Ananda and asks why nobody is caring for him. The monk answers: I'm of no use to the other monks, so they don't tend me.
The Buddha and Ananda fetch water, wash the man themselves, and lift him onto a bed.

teach.h: THE BEST CASE FOR THE OTHER MONKS.
teach.b: Then the Buddha calls the monks together. Did they have a case? Here's its best version.
They had come to practice, not to nurse. The man had done nothing for them. Every hour spent on him was an hour off their own path.

teach.h: NO MOTHER, NO FATHER HERE TO TEND YOU.
teach.b: The Buddha answers with a plain fact of their life: you have no mother and no father here to wait on you. If you don't wait on one another, who will?

teach.h: WAIT ON ME? WAIT ON THE SICK.
teach.b: Then a line monks would carry: whoever would wait on me should wait on the sick. Serving that man is how you serve the teacher.
And notice who did the washing first: not a junior monk assigned to the job, but the teacher himself, with water and his own hands. And the text doesn't stop at a scolding.

teach.h: A GOOD PATIENT, A GOOD NURSE.
teach.b: It lists what makes a sick person hard to nurse, like refusing medicine or not saying honestly how they feel, and what makes a good nurse, like one who serves from goodwill and not for gain. Both sides carry something.
That's the teaching: in the Buddha's community, care for a fellow member isn't extra credit; it's written into the rule.
At a desk, that's the colleague whose project isn't yours.

how: Buddhist monastic rules make caring for a sick fellow monk a duty of the community, and the texts describe the qualities of a good nurse and of a patient who is easy to care for.

o: giving a hand to the one nobody is responsible for
doing a teammate's whole task so they never learn it
only helping the people who have helped you before

games.q: the sick monk's story: tap the pairs.
p: left alone: no use to the others
why the monks must tend each other

he and Ananda fetched water and washed the monk themselves.
the text also lists what makes a patient hard to nurse
refusing medicine, not saying honestly how you feel. both sides carry something.

games.q: a new teammate keeps asking you basic questions while you're on deadline. your coworker says 'she's not our problem.' what's the strongest form of his side, and the Buddha's reply?
o: his side: your own work matters. the reply: if we don't tend each other, who will?
his side: she's lazy. the reply: lazy people deserve help most of all.
his side: it's not your role. the reply: then wait until she's officially assigned.
games.why: the monks' case was real: they had their own practice. the Buddha's answer: no mother, no father here; whoever would wait on me should wait on the sick.

practice: Bring to mind one person near you who's struggling and isn't quite anyone's job. Name the one small help within reach from where you sit, and the one thing that usually stops you from giving it.
Then rest your attention on that person until the bell.
